scope: Genesis 29–31, all 133 public verses; Genesis 31:55 ET is Gen 32:1 HT. Prior revisions remain unchanged.

source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of the exact UTF-8 <verse ...>...</verse> substring, including markup, whitespace, written forms, and any reading notes. No XML reserialization or Hebrew normalization.
source.public_versification_note: English Genesis 31:55 is bound to Hebrew Gen 32:1, whose original XML record includes the note KJV:Gen.31.55.

delta_method: F0 retained wording; F1 lexical; F2 syntax/idiom; F3 consequential interpretive, textual, social, or versification choice. These are editorial assessments, separate from similarity scores. Independent review has not occurred.

verses.rationale: Render the idiom lifted his feet as renewed travel without making the narrator explain Jacob’s mood; retain the regional designation.
verses.before: Then Jacob lifted his feet and went to the land of the sons of the east.
verses.after: Jacob continued his journey and reached the land of the eastern peoples.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob lifted his feet and went to the land of the sons of the east.

verses.rationale: Recast the repeated look presentation into a visible scene while retaining three flocks, their purpose, and the large stone.
verses.before: And he looked, and look, a well in the field, and look, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for from that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the mouth of the well was large.
verses.after: He saw a well in a field. Three flocks of sheep were lying beside it because the flocks were watered from that well. A large stone covered the well’s opening.
verses.tsw_comparator: And he looked, and behold, a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for from that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the mouth of the well was large.

verses.rationale: Make the customary sequence and implied shepherds explicit; preserve the repeated stone/opening wording.
verses.before: When all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
verses.after: When all the flocks gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone away from the well’s opening and water the sheep. Then they would return the stone to its place over the opening.
verses.tsw_comparator: When all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.

verses.rationale: Identify the addressed men from context and preserve Jacob’s courteous kinship address and their origin.
verses.before: Jacob said to them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”
verses.after: Jacob asked the shepherds, “My brothers, where are you from?” “We are from Haran,” they answered.
verses.tsw_comparator: Jacob said to them, “My brothers, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”

verses.rationale: Clarify the broad Hebrew son relationship from the genealogy while retaining Laban and Nahor rather than silently omitting the ancestry.
verses.before: He said to them, “Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.”
verses.after: “Do you know Laban, Nahor’s grandson?” he asked. “We do,” they answered.
verses.tsw_comparator: He said to them, “Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.”

verses.rationale: Retain the repeated shalom question and answer as well-being and introduce Rachel in the shepherds’ speech.
verses.before: He said to them, “Is it well with him?” They said, “It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep.”
verses.after: “Is he well?” Jacob asked. “He is well,” they said. “Here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep.”
verses.tsw_comparator: He said to them, “Is it well with him?” They said, “It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep.”

verses.rationale: Render the day-is-great idiom naturally while preserving his three-part proposal.
verses.before: He said, “Look, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them.”
verses.after: Jacob said, “There is still plenty of daylight. It is not time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep, then take them out to graze.”
verses.tsw_comparator: He said, “Behold, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them.”

verses.rationale: Preserve the stated inability, its two prerequisites, and the recurring action at the well.
verses.before: But they said, “We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep.”
verses.after: “We cannot,” they answered, “until all the flocks have gathered and the stone is rolled away from the well’s opening. Then we can water the sheep.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But they said, “We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep.”

verses.rationale: Keep Rachel’s work explicit and avoid reducing roah to an identity label when the sentence describes her action.
verses.before: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess.
verses.after: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep. She was tending the flock.
verses.tsw_comparator: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess.

verses.rationale: Retain the thrice-repeated maternal kinship connection while varying it naturally after establishing Laban as Jacob’s uncle.
verses.before: Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother’s brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the mouth of the well and watered the flock of Laban his mother’s brother.
verses.after: When Jacob saw Rachel, daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and saw Laban’s sheep, he went to the well, rolled the stone away, and watered his uncle’s flock.
verses.tsw_comparator: Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother’s brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the mouth of the well and watered the flock of Laban his mother’s brother.

verses.rationale: Keep both the greeting kiss and audible weeping without supplying the cause of his emotion.
verses.before: Then Jacob kissed Rachel and lifted up his voice and wept.
verses.after: Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob kissed Rachel and lifted up his voice and wept.

verses.rationale: Render the broad brother term as relative while making Jacob’s exact maternal identity explicit.
verses.before: Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s kinsman, and that he was Rebekah’s son, and she ran and told her father.
verses.after: Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s relative and Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s kinsman, and that he was Rebekah’s son, and she ran and told her father.

verses.rationale: Preserve Laban’s sequence of welcome and the open-ended all-these-matters report without inventing its contents.
verses.before: As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things,
verses.after: When Laban heard the news about his sister’s son Jacob, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him home. Jacob told Laban everything that had happened.
verses.tsw_comparator: As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things,

verses.rationale: Keep the concrete kinship idiom and the month-of-days duration.
verses.before: and Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh!” And he stayed with him a month.
verses.after: Laban said, “You truly are my own bone and flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for a full month.
verses.tsw_comparator: and Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh!” And he stayed with him a month.

verses.rationale: Make the deliberative question and proposed wage explicit; relative conveys the broad brother address.
verses.before: Then Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what will your wages be?”
verses.after: Then Laban said to Jacob, “Should you work for me without pay because you are my relative? Tell me what your wages should be.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?”

verses.rationale: Retain age order because it controls Laban’s later defense and the narrative reversal.
verses.before: Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
verses.after: Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah and the younger Rachel.
verses.tsw_comparator: Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.

verses.rationale: Choose gentle for the ambiguous rakkot without implying weak eyesight; preserve the explicit description of Rachel’s form and appearance.
verses.before: Leah’s eyes were soft, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
verses.after: Leah’s eyes were gentle, while Rachel was lovely in figure and appearance.
verses.tsw_comparator: Leah’s eyes were soft, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.

verses.rationale: Keep love as the reason for Jacob’s named seven-year offer and retain Rachel’s younger-daughter status.
verses.before: Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.”
verses.after: Jacob loved Rachel. He said, “I will work for you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.”

verses.rationale: Preserve Laban’s noncommittal comparative wording rather than turning it into an explicit acceptance formula.
verses.before: Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to another man; stay with me.”
verses.after: Laban answered, “It is better for me to give her to you than to another man. Stay with me.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to another man; stay with me.”

verses.rationale: Keep the love-duration comparison without adding that the years passed quickly or that the price was insignificant.
verses.before: So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.
verses.after: Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, but because he loved her, they seemed like only a few days to him.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.

verses.rationale: Render the sexual euphemism plainly in Jacob’s direct request while retaining wife and completion of service.
verses.before: Then Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed.”
verses.after: Jacob said to Laban, “My time is complete. Give me my wife so I may sleep with her.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed.”

verses.rationale: Keep the public gathering and wedding feast without adding ritual details absent from the verse.
verses.before: So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast.
verses.after: Laban gathered all the people of the place and held a feast.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast.

verses.rationale: Name both agents and render the sexual euphemism plainly; leave the mechanism and Leah’s agency unstated as in the source.
verses.before: But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her.
verses.after: But that evening Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her.
verses.tsw_comparator: But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her.

verses.rationale: Make Zilpah’s enslaved status and transfer between Laban and Leah explicit rather than presenting voluntary domestic employment.
verses.before: Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.
verses.after: Laban gave his enslaved woman Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her slave woman.
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.

verses.rationale: Retain the narrator’s sudden behold and Jacob’s accusation, including the repeated deception root from the preceding family story.
verses.before: And in the morning, look, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?”
verses.after: In the morning—there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, “What have you done to me? Didn’t I work for you for Rachel? Why did you deceive me?”
verses.tsw_comparator: And in the morning, behold, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?”

verses.rationale: Keep Laban’s local-custom defense and firstborn language, which echoes the older-younger conflict in Jacob’s own family.
verses.before: Laban said, “It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.
verses.after: Laban answered, “In our place, the younger daughter is not given before the firstborn.
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban said, “It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.

verses.rationale: Interpret the seven as the bridal week from the immediate fulfillment in verse 28; retain the collective we and further labor demand.
verses.before: Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years.”
verses.after: Complete this daughter’s wedding week, and we will give you the other one too, in return for another seven years of work for me.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years.”

verses.rationale: Identify Leah as the first demonstrative’s referent and preserve the timing that Rachel is given before the second seven years are completed.
verses.before: Jacob did so and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.
verses.after: Jacob agreed and completed Leah’s wedding week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
verses.tsw_comparator: Jacob did so and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.

verses.rationale: Make Bilhah’s enslaved status and transfer explicit, parallel to Zilpah in verse 24.
verses.before: Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.
verses.after: Laban gave his enslaved woman Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her slave woman.
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.

verses.rationale: Keep the sexual relationship, unequal love, and additional service distinct without excusing the household’s hierarchy.
verses.before: So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.
verses.after: Jacob slept with Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He worked for Laban another seven years.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.

verses.rationale: Retain the strong source word hated rather than reducing Leah’s condition to a neutral comparison; render barrenness as inability without blame.
verses.before: When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
verses.after: When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, while Rachel was unable to conceive.
verses.tsw_comparator: When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.

verses.rationale: Preserve Leah’s own interpretation, the seeing wordplay, suffering, and hope for her husband’s love.
verses.before: Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, “Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”
verses.after: Leah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Reuben, saying, “The LORD has seen my suffering. Now my husband will love me.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, “Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”

verses.rationale: Keep hearing, hatred, gift, and the name association in Leah’s voice.
verses.before: She conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also.” And she called his name Simeon.
verses.after: She conceived again and gave birth to a son. “The LORD heard that I am hated,” she said, “and he has given me this son too.” So she named him Simeon.
verses.tsw_comparator: She conceived again and bore a son, and said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also.” And she called his name Simeon.

verses.rationale: Preserve attached as the name wordplay and the passive naming form, whose namer is not specified.
verses.before: Again she conceived and bore a son and said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi.
verses.after: She conceived again and gave birth to a son. “At last my husband will become attached to me,” she said, “because I have borne him three sons.” That is why he was named Levi.
verses.tsw_comparator: Again she conceived and bore a son and said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi.

verses.rationale: Keep Leah’s changed focus on praise, the Judah word association, and the pause in births.
verses.before: And she conceived again and bore a son and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.
verses.after: She conceived once more and gave birth to a son. “This time I will praise the LORD,” she said. So she named him Judah. Then she stopped giving birth.
verses.tsw_comparator: And she conceived again and bore a son and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.

verses.rationale: Retain Rachel’s infertility, envy, demand, and death language without diagnosing her emotion.
verses.before: When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. And she said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die.”
verses.after: Rachel saw that she had borne Jacob no children, and she envied her sister. She told Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die!”
verses.tsw_comparator: When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. And she said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I shall die.”

verses.rationale: Keep Jacob’s anger and his attribution of fertility to God; preserve the concrete fruit-of-the-womb idiom.
verses.before: Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?”
verses.after: Jacob became furious with Rachel. “Am I in God’s place?” he said. “God has withheld the fruit of the womb from you.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?”

verses.rationale: Keep Bilhah’s enslaved status, the sexual arrangement, the knees ritual image, and Rachel’s building-family language; add no consent.
verses.before: Then she said, “See, here is my servant Bilhah. Go in to her, so that she may bear upon my knees and that through her I too may have children.”
verses.after: Rachel said, “Here is my slave woman Bilhah. Sleep with her so she can give birth on my knees, and I too may build a family through her.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then she said, “See, here is my servant Bilhah. Go in to her, so that she may bear upon my knees and that through her I too may have children.”

verses.rationale: Preserve both wife status and enslavement, and render the sexual euphemism directly without implying Bilhah chose the arrangement.
verses.before: So she gave him Bilhah her servant as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.
verses.after: Rachel gave Bilhah, her slave woman, to Jacob as a wife, and he slept with her.
verses.tsw_comparator: So she gave him Bilhah her servant as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.

verses.rationale: Retain the clear existing sentence: Bilhah remains the acting mother and Jacob the named father.
verses.before: Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
verses.after: Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.

verses.rationale: Render dananni as favorable judgment while keeping Rachel’s claim to the child and the Dan wordplay in her voice.
verses.before: Then Rachel said, “God has judged me and has also heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan.
verses.after: Rachel said, “God has judged in my favor. He has heard my voice and given me a son.” So she named him Dan.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Rachel said, “God has judged me and has also heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan.

verses.rationale: Retain Bilhah’s identity and status, the repeated conception, and second-son sequence.
verses.before: Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
verses.after: Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
verses.tsw_comparator: Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.

verses.rationale: Render struggles-of-God as an intensifier without claiming the struggle was divinely commanded; retain rivalry and name wordplay.
verses.before: Then Rachel said, “With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed.” So she called his name Naphtali.
verses.after: Rachel said, “I have struggled mightily with my sister, and I have prevailed.” So she named him Naphtali.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Rachel said, “With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed.” So she called his name Naphtali.

verses.rationale: Keep Leah’s motive, Zilpah’s enslavement, and the imposed wife status parallel to Bilhah.
verses.before: When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
verses.after: When Leah saw that she had stopped giving birth, she gave her slave woman Zilpah to Jacob as a wife.
verses.tsw_comparator: When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.

verses.rationale: Retain Zilpah as the mother and her enslaved status rather than erasing her from the birth notice.
verses.before: Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a son.
verses.after: Zilpah, Leah’s slave woman, bore Jacob a son.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a son.

verses.rationale: Follow the recorded traditional reading, two words meaning good fortune has come, and retain the Gad wordplay.
verses.before: Then Leah said, “Good fortune has come!” So she called his name Gad.
verses.after: Leah said, “Good fortune has come!” So she named him Gad.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Leah said, “Good fortune has come!” So she called his name Gad.

verses.rationale: Preserve the mother, status, father, and sequence in the compact notice.
verses.before: Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a second son.
verses.after: Zilpah, Leah’s slave woman, bore Jacob a second son.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a second son.

verses.rationale: Keep both noun and verb forms of the happiness wordplay and the gender-specific daughters/women reference.
verses.before: Then Leah said, “Happy am I! For women will call me happy.” So she called his name Asher.
verses.after: Leah said, “How happy I am! Women will call me happy.” So she named him Asher.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Leah said, “Happy am I! For women will call me happy.” So she called his name Asher.

verses.rationale: Preserve season, finder, plant, recipient, and Rachel’s request without asserting the plants’ intended effect.
verses.before: In the days of wheat harvest Reuben went and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to Leah his mother. Then Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”
verses.after: During the wheat harvest, Reuben went out and found mandrakes in the field. He brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”
verses.tsw_comparator: In the days of wheat harvest Reuben went and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to Leah his mother. Then Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

verses.rationale: Keep Leah’s accusation and Rachel’s bargaining over Jacob’s sexual access as their speech; identify Jacob without endorsing ownership.
verses.before: But she said to her, “Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband? Would you also take my son’s mandrakes?” Rachel said, “Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”
verses.after: Leah answered, “Was taking my husband such a small thing? Will you take my son’s mandrakes too?” Rachel said, “Then Jacob may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But she said to her, “Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband? Would you also take my son’s mandrakes?” Rachel said, “Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”

verses.rationale: Render the emphatic hire language and obligatory claim plainly while leaving the arrangement’s troubling agency visible.
verses.before: When Jacob came from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You must come in to me, for I have surely hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he lay with her that night.
verses.after: When Jacob came in from the fields that evening, Leah went to meet him. “You must sleep with me,” she said. “I have paid for you with my son’s mandrakes.” So Jacob slept with her that night.
verses.tsw_comparator: When Jacob came from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You must come in to me, for I have surely hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he lay with her that night.

verses.rationale: Retain divine hearing and the fifth-son count without crediting the mandrakes.
verses.before: God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
verses.after: God listened to Leah. She conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
verses.tsw_comparator: And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.

verses.rationale: Keep Leah’s interpretation, slave woman, and wages/name wordplay as her claim rather than the narrator’s judgment.
verses.before: Then Leah said, “God has given me my wages because I gave my servant to my husband.” So she called his name Issachar.
verses.after: Leah said, “God has given me my wages because I gave my slave woman to my husband.” So she named him Issachar.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Leah said, “God has given me my wages because I gave my servant to my husband.” So she called his name Issachar.

verses.rationale: Retain the clear existing compact birth notice and exact ordinal count.
verses.before: Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
verses.after: Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.

verses.rationale: Choose honor for the difficult name-related verb while retaining gift, hope, six sons, and Leah’s own interpretation.
verses.before: Then Leah said, “God has endowed me with a good gift. Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” So she called his name Zebulun.
verses.after: Leah said, “God has given me a good gift. Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” So she named him Zebulun.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Leah said, “God has endowed me with a good gift. Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” So she called his name Zebulun.

verses.rationale: Keep Dinah’s birth and naming explicit without implying she was the only daughter ever born.
verses.before: Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.
verses.after: Afterward Leah gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
verses.tsw_comparator: Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.

verses.rationale: Retain remembered as attentive covenantal action and repeat God as the source does.
verses.before: Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.
verses.after: Then God remembered Rachel. God listened to her and opened her womb.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.

verses.rationale: Keep Rachel’s disgrace language as her culturally situated experience, not a narrator’s verdict about infertility.
verses.before: And she conceived and bore a son and said, “God has taken away my reproach.”
verses.after: She conceived and gave birth to a son. She said, “God has taken away my disgrace.”
verses.tsw_comparator: And she conceived and bore a son and said, “God has taken away my reproach.”

verses.rationale: Keep selective use with stronger animals and the repeated sight/mating language.

verses.rationale: Retain doubled intensification, property language, enslaved people, and all livestock categories without softening the social reality.

verses.rationale: Keep the sons’ repeated accusation in their voice and render kabod here as wealth without making it objective fact.

verses.rationale: Retain return, ancestral land, kindred, and presence promise; family is broader than birthplace here.

verses.after: Jacob became angry and confronted Laban. “What is my offense?” he demanded. “What sin have I committed that you pursued me so fiercely?
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Jacob became angry and rebuked Laban. Jacob said to Laban, “What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?

verses.rationale: Retain the tactile search, public evidence demand, two groups, and adjudication request.
verses.before: For you have felt through all my goods. What have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us.
verses.after: You have felt through all my possessions. What have you found that belongs to your household? Put it here before my relatives and yours, and let them decide between us.
verses.tsw_comparator: For you have felt through all my goods. What have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us.

verses.rationale: Preserve duration, reproductive care, and Jacob’s claimed restraint from the flock.
verses.before: These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.
verses.after: I was with you for twenty years. Your ewes and female goats did not miscarry, and I did not eat the rams from your flock.
verses.tsw_comparator: These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.

verses.rationale: Render the bearing-of-loss verb as absorbing liability and preserve Laban’s day/night repayment demand.
verses.before: What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss myself. From my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.
verses.after: I did not bring you animals torn by predators; I absorbed the loss myself. You demanded repayment from me whether an animal was stolen by day or by night.
verses.tsw_comparator: What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss myself. From my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.

verses.rationale: Keep bodily cost and paired day/night conditions in terse parallel clauses.
verses.before: By day the heat consumed me and the cold by night, and sleep fled from my eyes.
verses.after: By day the heat consumed me, and by night the cold. Sleep fled from my eyes.
verses.tsw_comparator: By day the heat consumed me and the cold by night, and sleep fled from my eyes.

verses.rationale: Preserve all three numbers and work-for-daughters language as Jacob’s accusation; repeat ten times consistently.
verses.before: These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.
verses.after: For twenty years I served in your household: fourteen years for your two daughters and six for your flock. Yet you changed my wages ten times.
verses.tsw_comparator: These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.

verses.rationale: Retain the distinctive divine title Fear of Isaac and legal force of rebuke/decide; keep suffering and labor as what God saw.
verses.before: If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night.”
verses.after: If my father’s God—the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac—had not been with me, you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my suffering and the labor of my hands, and last night he decided the case.”
verses.tsw_comparator: If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night.”

verses.rationale: Preserve Laban’s sweeping ownership claims as speech, including women, children, animals, and property; do not validate them narratively.
verses.before: Then Laban answered and said to Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do today for these my daughters or for their children whom they have borne?
verses.after: Laban answered Jacob, “These daughters are my daughters, these children my children, and these flocks my flocks. Everything you see is mine. But what can I do today to these daughters of mine or to the children they have borne?
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Laban answered and said to Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do today for these my daughters or for their children whom they have borne?

verses.rationale: Retain both parties, covenant, and witness function without turning a boundary agreement into affection.
verses.before: Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between you and me.”
verses.after: Come now, let you and me make a covenant, and let it serve as a witness between us.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between you and me.”

verses.rationale: Keep the single stone and standing-pillar action, echoing the Bethel pillar.
verses.before: So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
verses.after: Jacob took a stone and set it upright as a pillar.
verses.tsw_comparator: So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.

verses.rationale: Preserve relatives, communal gathering, heap construction, and meal location.
verses.before: Jacob said to his kinsmen, “Gather stones.” And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
verses.after: Then Jacob told his relatives, “Gather stones.” They piled the stones into a heap and ate there beside it.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Jacob said to his kinsmen, “Gather stones.” And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.

verses.rationale: Retain both Aramaic and Hebrew-related names, whose shared witness-heap meaning is explained in vocabulary.
verses.before: Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
verses.after: Laban called the heap Jegar-sahadutha, while Jacob called it Galeed.
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.

verses.rationale: Keep Laban’s witness declaration and the place-name explanation.
verses.before: Laban said, “This heap is a witness between you and me today.” Therefore its name was called Galeed,
verses.after: Laban said, “This heap is a witness between you and me today.” That is why it was named Galeed.
verses.tsw_comparator: Laban said, “This heap is a witness between you and me today.” Therefore its name was called Galeed,

verses.rationale: Preserve watch/watchpost wordplay and mutual absence; do not recast this wary boundary as a sentimental blessing.
verses.before: and Mizpah, for he said, “May the LORD watch between you and me when we are hidden from one another.
verses.after: It was also called Mizpah, because Laban said, “May the LORD watch between you and me when we are out of each other’s sight.
verses.tsw_comparator: and Mizpah, for he said, “May the LORD watch between you and me when we are hidden from one another.

verses.rationale: Keep the warning against affliction and additional wives, human absence, and divine witness; leave Laban’s inconsistency visible.
verses.before: If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, though no one is with us, see, God is witness between you and me.”
verses.after: If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives in addition to them, even though no one else is with us, remember: God is witness between you and me.”
verses.tsw_comparator: If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, though no one is with us, see, God is witness between you and me.”

verses.rationale: Retain both markers and the repeated boundary positioning.
verses.before: Then Laban said to Jacob, “See this heap and the pillar, which I have set between you and me.
verses.after: Laban continued, “Look at this heap and this pillar that I have set between you and me.
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Laban said to Jacob, “See this heap and the pillar, which I have set between you and me.

verses.rationale: Preserve reciprocal boundary and explicit harmful purpose; do not claim an absolute ban on all future crossing.
verses.before: This heap is a witness, and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass beyond this heap to you, and you will not pass beyond this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm.
verses.after: This heap and pillar are witnesses: I will not cross beyond this heap toward you, and you will not cross beyond this heap and pillar toward me, to do harm.
verses.tsw_comparator: This heap is a witness, and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass beyond this heap to you, and you will not pass beyond this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm.

verses.rationale: Reflect the plural Hebrew judge and Laban’s polytheistic formulation while distinguishing Jacob’s oath by the Fear of Isaac.
verses.before: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
verses.after: May the God of Abraham and the god of Nahor—the gods of their father—judge between us.” Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
verses.tsw_comparator: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.

verses.rationale: Keep sacrifice, communal bread/meal, kinship group, and overnight stay without specifying the sacrifice type.
verses.before: Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. They ate bread and spent the night in the hill country.
verses.after: Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to share the meal. They ate and spent the night on the mountain.
verses.tsw_comparator: And Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. They ate bread and spent the night in the hill country.

verses.rationale: Map public 31:55 to Hebrew 32:1, including its embedded English-versification note; render sons as grandchildren because these are Jacob’s children.
verses.before: Early in the morning Laban rose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned to his place.
verses.after: Early the next morning Laban kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them. Then he left and returned home.
verses.tsw_comparator: Early in the morning Laban rose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned to his place.
